summary: Portage River Light at Jacobsville, Michigan: lit 1856, rebuilt 1869, retired 1920. Now a private home under restoration, closed to visitors.

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds, tower and dwelling closed to visitors (LighthouseFriends). Do not visit without the owners' permission.

events.note: Lit from the first tower, although the engineer had refused to accept the station as built to contract.
Tower and dwelling rebuilt from March 1869 appropriation; a temporary structure carried the light.
Light first shown from the new tower in the 1870 navigation season.
Changed on 15 August 1891 from fixed white with a red flash every two minutes to a red flash every minute.
Seawall about nine feet high and 100 feet long built south of the light.
Replaced by the Keweenaw Waterway light at the breakwater, first shown 1 August 1920.
Transferred to the State of Michigan for a planned park, 10 August 1932.
Reverted to the Coast Guard, 29 October 1948.
Sold at GSA auction, 25 November 1958, for $18,251. LighthouseFriends names Ray and Sylvia Joynt; Pepper names Joynt Automotive of Alma.
Bought by Mike and Cheri Ditty, who ran it as the Jacobsville Lighthouse Inn.
Inn operation ended in the fall of 2019.

corrections.why: The record's 9.8 m matches the USLHS figure of 32 ft from base to lantern centre (cite 3). LighthouseFriends and Pepper give the 1869 tower as about 51 ft (15.5 m) tall. Needs human review; the two measurements differ.
Pepper and the restorers' timeline say locally quarried sandstone; the USLHS record says brick. Needs human review.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1870 is the year the light was first shown from the new tower (Pepper; USLHS 'Year Tower Established 1870'). Construction was authorised in March 1869.
USLHS lists 'Open to Public: Yes', but LighthouseFriends and Pepper describe a private house with closed grounds. The story follows the private status.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on several points, all stated or left out in the story. (1) Tower material: Pepper and the restorers' timeline say local sandstone; USLHS says brick. (2) Tower height: LighthouseFriends says 51 ft and Pepper about 51 ft to the vent ball; USLHS gives 32 ft from base to lantern centre. (3) Lantern: LighthouseFriends says cast iron, Pepper says wood. (4) Lens flash: LighthouseFriends says the panels revolved every four minutes, Pepper says every two minutes, and the 1892 Board report says the pre-1891 light was a red flash every two minutes. Pepper alone describes a single white flash every minute. (5) 1865 keeper: Pepper names Samuel Stevenson as keeper when the pier light was added; USLHS has John B. Crebassa from 1865 and Samuel Stephenson 1857-1861. Not resolved. (6) 1958 buyer: Ray and Sylvia Joynt (LighthouseFriends) versus Joynt Automotive of Alma (Pepper). (7) Pepper's text has a typo, 'September 10, 1956', for 1856. (8) The restorers' timeline credits Orlando M. Poe with the 1869 design. No source I could read confirms this, so it is left out of the story. (9) The 1868 and 1869 Light-House Board reports were not in the local corpus; the 1868 inspector's words are quoted as LighthouseFriends prints them and paraphrased from Pepper. A primary check is needed. (10) Roster lines come from the USLHS place page; the match was by position (0.30 km) and name, and the place is the only USLHS place there. (11) Commissioner 1920 page printed p. 51 is confirmed by the page heading; the 1915 estimates are cited by scan page 90 only. The 1892 Board report is cited by scan page 546 with the printed page unconfirmed. (12) The 1899 and 1900 river-mouth lights are the Portage River range and pier lights, not the house light; the story keeps them apart. (13) No wreck or rescue tied to the house light was found in the sources read, so no wrecks key was written. (14) The current owners' site and the 2022 sale date come from the owners' own timeline and have not been checked against a public record. (15) No photos were mirrored or added; the LighthouseFriends photographs are copyright Kraig Anderson. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28 (Haiku 5.5): checked every footnoted sentence against the cached sources, and the corpus pages: 1892 Board report scan 546 (characteristic change, wording confirmed; printed page still unconfirmed); 1900 report scan 31 (several Portage River range and minor lights carried away by ice on 9 May 1900, confirmed); 1899 report scan 36 (confirmed); 1915 estimates scan 90, printed 85 (confirmed; the 1915 OCR 'eretedon' is quoted as printed); 1920 report scan 549, printed 51 (confirmed; the OCR reads 'unneressary' and the story quotes the printed word 'unnecessary'). Corrections in the story: 'Lighthouse Service' is now 'U.S. Lighthouse Society' (the roster and place record are the Society's); the $12,000 appropriation is cited to LighthouseFriends only; Pepper's 'Stevenson' is no longer equated with the roster's Stephenson; the 1892 change is now quoted in full, 'to a fixed white light, varied by a red flash, every minute'; the 51-foot figures are attributed separately (LighthouseFriends: tower; Pepper: vent ball above the foundation). Pepper's wording for the 1857 refusal is attributed to LighthouseFriends. The 2004 sale is reported by LighthouseFriends as an inn and by the owners' timeline as an attempt at bed and breakfast; the story follows LighthouseFriends and does not settle it. The owners' site is the only source for the 2022 sale and the restoration.
